The North Coast Province spans approximately 2,100 km² and is underlain by the North Coast Limestone aquifer system, the most productive and extensive aquifer system in Puerto Rico. The North Coast Limestone and South Coastal Alluvial Plain aquifer systems account for nearly 70% of all groundwater withdrawals on the island. The North Coast Limestone aquifer system covers roughly 2,000 km², with the most intensive groundwater development occurring within an 800 km² area between the Río Grande de Arecibo and the Río de la Plata. This region is of particular concern for the use of groundwater, which serves as a critical source of water for both domestic and industrial purposes. In 1985, groundwater withdrawals in this area were estimated at 280,000 cubic meters per day (m³/d), supplying 100% of the water used by self-supplied industries and approximately 85% of public water supplies. By 2005, withdrawals had declined to 150,000 m³/d, reflecting changes in demand, resource availability, or water management practices (Gómez-Gómez et al. 2014). The North Coast Groundwater Province is divided into three limestone aquifer systems: (1) from the West Coast to the Río Grande de Arecibo area, (2) from Río Grande de Arecibo to Río de la Plata, and (3) from Río de la Plata to Río Espíritu Santo, the latter of which lies beneath San Juan. Generalized geology and cross sections from the San Juan and Barceloneta areas show that the surface is primarily composed of unconsolidated Quaternary alluvial and other surficial deposits, overlying older Cretaceous-Tertiary limestone and terrigenous clastic rocks. Several deep exploration wells were analyzed across the North Coast of Puerto Rico, including 15 North Coast wells, an Interaquifer System well, hydrocarbon Commonwealth of Puerto Rico (CPR) CPR-4 well, and the Toa Baja Scientific Drillhole (Figure 5). Thermal studies, including the Toa Baja Scientific Drillhole analysis (Anderson and Larue, 1991), estimated heat flow between 23 and 37 milliwatts per square meter (mW/m²) from depths of 800 to 2,500 m, with a peak of 90 mW/m² observed at a mineralized zone beneath a volcanic sill or flow, before decreasing to 50 mW/m².
